title: Devanagari
hook: two real answers to how a beginner should start
tomorrow: where else can a vowel sign hide on a letter?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devanagari's virama: a small stroke that cancels a letter's a, so jagat, the world, can end on a t. Today, an argument teachers really have.

Every phone can type Sanskrit in English letters. Karma, yoga, namaste: nobody needs a new alphabet to read those. So should a beginner even bother with Devanagari, or just learn Sanskrit in Roman letters, with a few marks for the long vowels? It sounds like a question about fonts. Ask two Sanskrit teachers, and it turns out to be a question about what the language is.
screen: `SANSKRIT IN ENGLISH LETTERS.` → `WHY A NEW ALPHABET?` → `TWO TEACHERS, TWO ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: One side says: start in the script. Devanagari isn't a costume on the sounds; it's laid out by the sounds. The built-in a, the virama, the short i that's drawn first: learn them, and the script quietly teaches how Sanskrit works while you read. And the printed Gita, the temple wall, a grandmother's prayer book open to you as they are, not as someone transcribed them. The other side says: start in Roman letters, the kind scholars use, with a small bar over the long vowels. Sanskrit has been written in more than one script, so no single script is the language. Get to the verses sooner, while the wanting is fresh, and let the script come once you love what it carries. Some who hold this view hear something reverent in it: the sound is the scripture, and letters of any kind are its clothes. Both sides want the same thing, a reader who can hear the verse. They differ on the door. Some learners end up using both, Roman letters for the first weeks, Devanagari as soon as the shapes stop looking strange. This path shows both, side by side.
screen: `START IN THE SCRIPT: IT TEACHES THE SOUNDS.` · `START IN ROMAN LETTERS: REACH THE VERSES.` · `THE SOUND IS THE SCRIPTURE.` · `SAME GOAL, DIFFERENT DOOR.`

segments.voice: Look at any sign or label near you written in a script you can't read, or, if there isn't one, at the shapes of the letters on your own screen as if you couldn't read them. Let them be only lines and curves for a while, and notice the moment meaning tries to come back. Then let it.
Devanagari: one of the scripts Sanskrit is written in, and, for many teachers, the door into how its sounds work.
Keep this: Devanagari, one of two doors into Sanskrit, with the same verse waiting on the other side. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sanskrit courses differ: some teach Devanagari from the first lesson, others begin with romanized Sanskrit (with marks for long vowels and special sounds) and add the script later, and some textbooks print both on facing lines.

fork.setup: your friend swears by learning Devanagari first and calls Roman letters lazy. what's the best case for the other side?
options: no one script is Sanskrit itself, and reaching the verses sooner keeps the love alive.
Devanagari is too hard for anyone who didn't grow up with it.
Roman letters were the original way Sanskrit was written.
fork.reveal: the Roman-first view rests on two points: Sanskrit has worn more than one script, and getting to the verses early keeps a learner going. the strongest case is never that the script is too hard.
